content: Recent advancements in research have significantly enhanced our understanding of the biology of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and the pathogenesis of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). The development of sensitive tools to monitor HIV replication in infected individuals has allowed for accurate assessment of disease progression risk and mortality, as well as direct evaluation of the efficacy of anti-HIV therapies. When used appropriately, combinations of newly available, potent antiviral therapies can achieve prolonged suppression of detectable HIV replication levels and mitigate the virus's natural tendency to develop drug-resistant variants. However, as antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV infection has become more effective, it has also grown increasingly complex. It is essential for healthcare providers to stay informed about recent research advances to ensure that these therapies are utilized in ways that most effectively improve the health and extend the lives of individuals living with HIV. To facilitate the optimal use of rapidly accumulating knowledge about HIV pathogenesis and treatment, the Office of AIDS Research at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) convened the NIH Panel to Define Principles of Therapy of HIV Infection. This panel was tasked with establishing essential scientific principles to guide the effective use of antiretroviral therapies and viral load testing in clinical practice. Based on a thorough review of the latest data, the panel outlined eleven principles addressing critical issues in the treatment of HIV infection. These principles form the scientific foundation for specific treatment recommendations made by the Panel on Clinical Practices for the Treatment of HIV Infection, sponsored by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation. The reports from both panels are included in this publication. Together, they summarize new data and provide both the scientific basis and specific guidelines for treating individuals with HIV. This information is intended to benefit healthcare providers, HIV-infected individuals, educators, public health authorities, and organizations funding medical care for people living with HIV. It is important to note that the information presented may not necessarily reflect FDA approval or approved labeling for specific products or indications. Over the past two years, remarkable progress has been made in developing antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV infection and in measuring HIV plasma RNA (viral load) to guide the use of these drugs. The use of ART, combined with the prevention of specific HIV-related opportunistic infections (OIs), has led to dramatic reductions in the incidence of OIs, hospitalizations, and deaths among individuals with HIV. However, the rapid pace of advancements in this field has posed significant challenges for healthcare providers, patients, and institutions responsible for funding these therapies. To address these challenges, the Office of AIDS Research, the NIH, and the HHS, in collaboration with the Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation, have taken a leadership role in formulating scientific principles (NIH Panel) and developing guidelines (HHS/Kaiser Panel) for the use of antiretroviral drugs. These efforts are presented in this report, which is primarily targeted at providers caring for individuals with HIV but is also intended for patients, payors, pharmacists, and public health officials. The report consists of two articles. The first, Report of the NIH Panel to Define Principles of Therapy of HIV Infection, provides the foundation for the use of antiretroviral drugs. The second, Guidelines for the Use of Antiretroviral Agents in HIV-Infected Adults and Adolescents, offers specific recommendations on when to start, how to monitor, and when to change therapy, as well as which drug combinations to consider. Both articles include cross-references to facilitate access to related information. Tables and figures are included in the appendices following each article. While the principles are unlikely to change in the near future, the guidelines will evolve as new information and drugs become available. Copies of this document and updates are available from the CDC National AIDS Clearinghouse and the HIV/AIDS Treatment Information Service. Readers are encouraged to consult these resources regularly for updates to the guidelines. In summary, the past two years have brought significant advancements in both basic and clinical research on AIDS. The availability of more potent drugs to inhibit HIV replication has enabled the design of therapeutic strategies involving combinations of antiretroviral drugs that achieve prolonged and near-complete suppression of detectable HIV replication in many individuals. Additionally, sensitive and reliable measurements of plasma viral load have proven to be powerful predictors of disease progression and mortality risk, as well as reliable indicators of the antiviral activity of therapeutic agents. It is now critical to translate these scientific advances into actionable information that practitioners and patients can use to make informed decisions about utilizing new therapies and monitoring tools to achieve the greatest and most durable clinical benefits. This information will allow physicians to tailor more effective treatments for their patients and closely monitor their responses to specific antiretroviral regimens. A two-track process was initiated to address this need. The NIH sponsored the NIH Panel to Define Principles of Therapy of HIV Infection, which was tasked with delineating scientific principles based on the biology and pathogenesis of HIV infection and disease. These principles are intended to guide the effective use of antiretroviral therapy and viral load testing in clinical practice. The HHS and the Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation sponsored the Panel on Clinical Practices for the Treatment of HIV Infection, which developed recommendations for the clinical use of antiretroviral drugs and laboratory monitoring methods. Both documents—the NIH Panel's report and the HHS Panel's guidelines—are included in this report. Together, they summarize new data and provide both the scientific basis and specific guidelines for treating individuals with HIV. The goal of this report is to assist clinicians and patients in making informed decisions about treatment options to ensure that effective antiretroviral therapy is introduced before extensive immune system damage occurs, viral load monitoring is used as an essential tool, combinations of antiretroviral drugs are employed to suppress HIV replication below detectable levels, and patient adherence to complex regimens is encouraged through education and support. The NIH Panel included clinicians, researchers, public health officials, and community representatives. As part of its efforts, the panel held a two-day public meeting to hear presentations on topics such as the relationship between virus replication and disease progression, the ability of antiviral therapy to minimize HIV replication, the emergence of drug resistance, and the relationship between drug-induced changes in viral load and improved clinical outcomes. The principles and conclusions discussed in this report have been developed to enable practitioners and patients to make treatment decisions based on the most current research results. Insights into the pathogenesis of HIV disease will continue to accumulate rapidly, providing new targets for developing additional antiretroviral drugs and more effective treatment strategies. As such, these principles will require modification and elaboration as new information becomes available.
